messages.author: 64dd3e60f9213f7d
messages.subject: shading/coloring space
parts:
Hi all,

Does anybody know how to shade or color the space between two independent lines in a plot? For example between a and b:

i<-0:5
a<-exp(sqrt(i^2))
b<-exp(sqrt((i-1)^2))
plot(a,type="n")
lines(a,type="l",pch=2,col="red")
lines(b,type="l",pch=2,col="blue")

Best
Chris

messages.subject: Problems with character encoding
parts:
Hi everyone,

I have a problem with the encoding of the Santa Barbara Corpus (SCAE).
Specifically: The compilers state that the SCAE is UTF-8 encoded, but
when I load the data, it still contains encoded sequences in the output.
To give you an impression of what my current output looks like, here
are the first six lines form the first file (I have already separated
the sepakers from the content):

corpus.content[[1]][1:6]
[1] " ## So you don't need to go ## borrow equipment from anybody
\025%snd \"01\"_0_9210\025 to +/. \025%snd \"01\"_9210_9520\025 *"
[2] " ## to do the feet ? \025%snd \"01\"_9520_14100\025 *"
[3] " ## âŒˆ Do the hooves âŒ‰ ? *"
[4] " âŒŠ &=in long âŒ‹ &{l=YWN Well we're gonna have to find
somewhere to get &=ex ## something &=ex &}l=YWN . *"
[5] " # So âŒŠ Mae_A âŒ‹ +... *"
[6] " âŒˆ I'm gonna âŒ‰ &=ex +... *"

I have already specified the encoding parameter in scan, i.e. I
included encoding = "UTF-8". Also, I used
Encoding(corpus.content[[1]]) which tells me that the encoding is
unknown. I tried some other fixes but none worked, i.e. the characters
remained encoded in the output.
I'm sure I'm not the first one encountering this problem... So does
anyone know how to convert the encoding into actual characters?

Best
Martin

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Problems with character encoding
parts:
Hi all,
I am having the exact same problem. I am using CLAN and the CHAT-CA format and I cannot convert .CHA files to R without a lot of problems with character encoding like Martin has had due to the characters not being ASCII-based. I found an R script online to convert CHAT formatted CLAN transcripts here: http://www.mit.edu/~mekline/Resources/CLANtoR/CLANtoR.R but I still have problems with characters not working. I have contacted Brian MacWhinney at the TalkBank project and he informed me that .CHA files should not be directly converted (due to layered encoding) and that CLAN can output a plain-text version of the transcript that should be used. I have not had a chance to try this because I have not had a lot of time to experiment with and learn more about CLAN but I will need to figure this out eventually. Hopefully we can figure this out together.
I hope this helps,
Mackenzie Salt,
PhD Student, Cognitive Science of Language,
McMaster University

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Problems with character encoding
parts:
Hey R-onauts,

thanks for the suggestions and help John - it is much appreciated!
I think it had something to do with unicode vs utf-8, because the data
is much more what I want it to look like when converting it to unicode
(still not quite perfect though).
@Mackenzie: I thought about converting the cha files into txt files
but I don't want to use other environments (I pretty sure you could do
this much simpler using Python) as I want to have one script for the
entire analysis (including graphs and statz).

The result looks like this (here the speakers are not removed yet):

*LENOR:\t## So you don't need to go ## borrow equipment from anybody
\025%snd:"01"_0_9210\025
\tto +/. \025%snd:"01"_9210_9520\025
*LENOR:\t## to do the feet ? \025%snd:"01"_9520_14100\025
*LENOR:\t## ⌈ Do the hooves ⌉ ? \025%snd:"01"_14100_15780\025
*LYNNE:\t⌊ &=in:long ⌋ &{l=YWN Well \025%snd:"01"_15010_16780\025
\twe're gonna have to find somewhere \025%snd:"01"_16780_18320\025
\tto get \025%snd:"01"_18330_18850\025


Here is the code I used (FYI) (@Mackenzie: maybe it useful to you ;)).

###############################################################
### START
###############################################################
# Remove all lists from the current workspace
rm(list=ls(all=T))

# Load packages
library(tm)
library(stringr)
library(gsubfn)
library(plyr)
library(reshape)
library(Unicode)

# Setting options
options(stringsAsFactors = F)

# Setting parameters
# Specify pathname of the corpus
pathname = "C:\\Users\\admin\\Desktop\\CorpLing\\00 corpora
orginals\\SantaBarbara Corpus Spoken AmE\\SBCSAE\\data"

# Prepare for loading corpus
# Define the paths for the corpus files
corpus.files = list.files(path = pathname,
pattern = NULL,
all.files = T,
full.names = T,
recursive = T,
ignore.case = T,
include.dirs = T)

# Load and store corpus
LoadCorpusFiles <- function (X) {
corpus.tmp <- scan(X,

what = "char",
sep = "\n",

quiet = T,
encoding = "UTF-8")
}

corpus.tmp <- lapply(X = corpus.files, FUN = LoadCorpusFiles)

# Transform the encoding of the corpus files from unicode to UTF-8
corpus.tmp.z <- lapply(corpus.tmp, function(x) {
sapply(x, function(y) {
as.u_char(y)
} )
} )

# View results
corpus.tmp.z[[1]][10:16]

###############################################################

Best,
Martin

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Problems with character encoding
parts:
@Martin:
1) The corpus is here (as .trn files):
<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/sites/secure.lsit.ucsb.edu.ling.cms/files/sitefiles/research/SBC/SBCorpus.zip>.
These files are UTF-8 (acc. to Geany/Kate) ANSI as UTF-8 (acc. to
Notepad++).
Loading it with this line works fine:
a.trn.file <- scan("/home/stgries/Desktop/SBCorpus/TRN/SBC001.trn",
what=character(0), sep="\n", fileEncoding="UTF-8")

2) The corpus is here (as .cha files):
<http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/sites/secure.lsit.ucsb.edu.ling.cms/files/sitefiles/research/SBC/SBCSAE_chat.zip>.
These files are UTF-8 (acc. to Geany/Kate) ANSI as UTF-8 (acc. to
Notepad++).
Loading it with this line works fine:
a.cha.file <- scan("/home/stgries/Desktop/SBCSAE_chat/SBCSAE/SBC001.cha",
what=character(0), sep="\n", fileEncoding="UTF-8")
But since the files contain strange characters, the display on the
screen looks bad, but is in fact not. The omnipresent \025 for example
seems to be the "Negative Acknowledge Character", which why it's
octally represented as \025 and, in a hex editor as 15; see
<http://www.asciitable.com/> - but you can still search, replace,
everything in order to, say, clean things up first. For example, this
works:
grep("\025", a.cha.file[1:32], perl=TRUE)

3) > I was thinking that maybe I should delve into the issue of
unicode enconding and how to handle it in R

Always a good idea: <http://www.joelonsoftware.com/articles/Unicode.html>.

@Mackenzie
1) See above: the characters are IN the code and R handles them fine,
it's the display side of things that's the problem - searches etc.
will all work fine. (Obviously, because that's how this script you
refer to does it, too, and that script doesn't even take encodings
into consideration!)

2) With all due respect, I doubt very much Brian is right (with "CHA
files should not be directly converted (due to layered encoding)")
because my book actually has a section that deals directly with CHA
files. And if CHA files were regular text files rather than what they
are, it would be much easier - Firefox doesn't even recognize they are
text and considers them BIN files. The problem is more one of many of
these files containing weird characters to do stuff; one more reason
to not have to rely on overspecific tools that may or may not be able
to produce what one needs.

Cheers,

STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.author: dcf30cbeaf00af93
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Problems with character encoding
parts:
Hi Mackenzie

I don't know why Brian said that it's better not to directly convert .cha files
- they are just text, so if you are using UTF-8 on your machine (and any sane
person should be), and the .cha files are in UTF-8, there should be no problem.
We have been chopping them up and importing them into database tables with
zero problems (http://bangortalk.org.uk). Brian does sometimes give the
impression that .cha files are sacrosanct, but they're just text, and actually
quite nice to deal with.

::::On Thursday 22 August 2013 Stefan Th. Gries said::::

> The omnipresent \025 for example
> seems to be the "Negative Acknowledge Character", which why it's
> octally represented as \025 and, in a hex editor as 15;

This character is used to delimit the "sound-bullets" in .cha files. The
sound-bullets are time-marks that allow the CHAT application to play the audio
file and show the relevant line of text at the same time. This only works in
Windows and Mac OS X, because they use QuickTime (!), which doesn't run
properly in Linux.

But these characters are not a problem - either trim out the sound-bullets, eg
sed -ri “s/([\.\?\!]) .[0-9].*/\1/g” chatfile.cha
(put this in a loop if you need to do more than one file) or just ignore them.

I don't know what text editor you are using, but most competent ones should
show the character somehow (eg Kate and Gedit show it as 0015 in a square), so
it should be easy to deal with it.

--
Pob hwyl / Best wishes

Kevin Donnelly
kevindonnelly.org.uk
bangortalk.org.uk
